OpenAI today revealed how it will comply with the EU's AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to label AI-generated text in a machine-readable format. Here are the details.

Some background

A few months ago, Anthropic sparked controversy when it announced that, to comply with the EU AI Act, Claude would watermark text by slightly tweaking word choices.

In simple terms, Claude would periodically select from multiple semantically equivalent words based on a hidden pattern. Anthropic stressed that this mechanism has no actual impact on the meaning, quality, or readability of responses.

Anthropic also developed a detection tool that can identify this pattern in a piece of text to determine whether the content is likely to have originated from Claude.

Since Claude's watermark is produced using a secret belonging solely to Anthropic's system, this detection tool cannot be used to tell whether a piece of text came from OpenAI or other competitors.

At the height of the controversy, Anthropic stressed that Claude would not be the only one, noting that several other major AI providers were also rolling out labelling systems to meet EU requirements.

OpenAI today announced its own approach, which, while similar, is much smaller in both rollout scope and coverage.

OpenAI's text watermarking system

OpenAI stated that starting today, "API customers worldwide can choose to enable text watermarking on specified models"; as for ChatGPT and Codex users, "in the coming weeks, eligible text outputs in the EU region will be embedded with an invisible watermark".

In other words, for the API, text watermarking remains off by default for now; and for ChatGPT and Codex, it will initially only be enabled for eligible users in the EU region.

OpenAI has also opened up applications for its text watermark detection tool, but initially only approved researchers and professional institutions can use it, allowing the company to continuously evaluate and refine the technology.

Regarding accuracy, OpenAI is very clear that this detection technology still has significant limitations. It can produce false negatives and false positives, particularly with shorter texts or content in specific domains, "such as mathematics, where there is less flexibility in word choice".

Here is OpenAI's explanation of textGrain (its text watermarking technology):

The company also noted that, in addition to being harder to detect in shorter passages, the watermark is significantly weakened once it has been manually edited.

Interestingly, after comparing watermarked and non-watermarked text, OpenAI found that watermarked outputs actually scored slightly higher on several benchmarks, though the company said it found no significant difference in general performance.

Benchmark Unwatermarked text (Astra, max) Watermarked text (Astra, max) Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 49.57 points 49.76 points AutomationBench 34.09% 34.86% DeepSWE v1.1 72.80% 71.68% Terminal-Bench 4.0 53.90% 56.06% Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 56.90% 60.00% BrowseComp 87.92% 87.35% HealthBench Professional 64.27% 64.60% GPQA Diamond 94.44% 93.94%

OpenAI also stressed that, in addition to the issues of false positives and false negatives, watermarks "cannot measure the degree of human involvement", "cannot establish ownership or responsibility", "cannot identify user identity", and also "cannot verify the accuracy of content".

OpenAI added that "the absence of a watermark does not prove that content was created by a human".

Finally, the company said it expects to review its approach again as technology, standards, and research evidence evolve, while continuing to study how much watermarks can survive editing or translation, and whether they can more effectively distinguish between "AI-assisted" and "AI-generated".
